title: Research ethics
note: The Belmont Report (1979) rests US human-research ethics on three principles: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice. They are applied through informed consent, careful weighing of risks and benefits, and fair selection of participants. An IRB reviews studies before they begin.

read.title: Why the rules exist
text: Modern research ethics grew out of abuses. After World War II, the trials of Nazi doctors produced the Nuremberg Code, whose first principle is that voluntary consent is essential. In the United States, the Tuskegee study ran from 1932 to 1972: government researchers followed Black men with syphilis without treating them, even after penicillin became standard care.

Public outrage over Tuskegee led Congress to create a national commission, which issued the Belmont Report in 1979. It names three principles. Respect for persons means treating people as able to make their own choices and protecting those who can't fully do so, such as children. Beneficence means not harming people and weighing risks against benefits. Justice means that no group should bear the burdens of research while others reap its rewards.

Each principle has a practical form. Informed consent requires that people get the relevant information, understand it, and agree freely, without threats or excessive rewards. A systematic risk-benefit assessment asks whether the knowledge gained justifies what participants face. Fair selection keeps researchers from recruiting people just because they are easy to reach or to pressure.
Today, an Institutional Review Board checks these points before a study involving people can begin.
